After sending them in, I could not stay away from the places that held them. Somehow I felt the petitions had a better chance, that their situation was less hopeless, when I was nearby. Driven by this unreasonable anxiety and distress, I wandered the streets in the evenings, passing the offices and houses where I had left them. Even now, the dreary streets of western London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their rows of stern, closed mansions and long lines of lamps, make me sad because of that memory.

My daily visits to him were shorter now, and he was watched more closely. Thinking, or imagining, that they suspected I meant to bring him poison, I asked to be searched before sitting beside his bed. I told the officer who was always present that I would do anything to prove I had no hidden purpose. Nobody treated either of us unkindly. There was a duty to carry out, and they carried it out without cruelty. The officer always told me he was worse. Other sick prisoners in the room, and the prisoners who cared for them—criminals, but still capable of kindness, thank God!—always said the same.

As the days passed, I noticed more and more how peacefully he lay watching the white ceiling, with no light in his face. Sometimes something I said brightened it for an instant, but then the light faded again. At times he could barely speak, or could not speak at all. Then he answered by gently pressing my hand, and I learned to understand him very well.

Ten days had passed when I noticed a greater change than any I had seen before. His eyes were fixed on the door, and they brightened as I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said when I sat beside his bed, “I thought you were late. But I knew you couldn’t be.”

“It’s exactly the right time,” I said. “I waited at the gate.”

“You always wait at the gate, don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So I don’t lose a moment with you.”

“Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You’ve never abandoned me, dear boy.”

I squeezed his hand without speaking, unable to forget that I had once planned to abandon him.

“And the best thing of all,” he said, “is that you’ve felt more at ease with me since I’ve been under this dark cloud than you did when the sun was shining.

I moved alongside a broad fellow with a plump, good-natured face, intending to make friendly conversation and gather a few more scraps of information. But we had barely become acquainted before he began eagerly and clumsily working his way, in the time-honored manner, toward that same old anecdote—the one Sir Dinadan had told me when I got into trouble with Sir Sagramor and received his challenge because of it. I excused myself and fell back to the end of the procession, heavyhearted and ready to depart this troubled life, this valley of tears, this brief day of interrupted rest, clouds and storms, exhausting struggle and repetitive defeat. Yet I shrank from the change when I remembered how long eternity lasts, and how many people already there know that anecdote.

Early in the afternoon we caught up with another procession of pilgrims. This one had no merriment, no jokes or laughter, no playfulness, none of the happy silliness of either youth or age. Yet both were present: gray-haired old men and women, strong middle-aged men and women, young husbands and wives, little girls and boys, and three nursing babies. Even the children did not smile. Every face among these fifty people was downcast, marked by the fixed hopelessness born of long suffering and familiarity with despair. They were slaves. Chains ran from their shackled feet and wrists to thick leather belts around their waists. All except the children were also joined in single file, six feet apart, by one chain running from collar to collar along the whole line. They traveled on foot and had covered three hundred miles in eighteen days, surviving on miserly portions of the cheapest food scraps. Every night they had slept in their chains, huddled together like pigs. A few wretched rags hung on their bodies, but they could hardly be called clothed. Their irons had rubbed the skin from their ankles, leaving open, festering sores alive with worms. Their bare feet were torn, and every one of them limped. There had originally been a hundred of these unfortunate people, but about half had been sold during the journey. The trader who controlled them rode a horse and carried a whip with a short handle and a long, heavy lash that split into several knotted tails at the end. Whenever anyone staggered with pain or exhaustion, he slashed their shoulders with it to make them stand upright. He said nothing; the whip communicated his wishes well enough.

“But when I saw another’s love directed toward you; when I imagined you loved as something other than a holy emblem and image of beauty and goodness, or pictured you loving someone else more passionately than you loved me, the demon within me stirred. I sent your lover away, and from that hour I have had no peace. In vain I have pursued sleep and repose: my eyelids would not shut, and my blood remained in ceaseless turmoil. I awakened into a new existence as one who dies full of hope might awaken in Hell. I shall not stain your imagination with an account of my struggles, my rage against myself, and my despair. Let the unthinkable feelings of a guilty father remain veiled; the secrets of a heart in such agony must not be exposed to common view. Within me were tumult, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet also the most tender love. The first thing to rouse my firm determination to overcome my passion and give my child her father back was the sight of your deep, compassionate sorrow. That brought me here. I believed that if I revived the grief I had felt at your mother’s death, together with the countless memories of her that had slept for seventeen years, all love for her child would die. In a heroic impulse I resolved to come alone, to leave you, the life of my life, and see you no more until I could do so without guilt. But it could not be: I valued my strength too highly, or my love too little. I would surely have died had you not hurried to me. Would that my life had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must offer my final confession. I was miserably deceived in thinking I could master my love for you; I never shall. The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived, seems only to have strengthened it. In my madness I dared tell myself: Diana died to bring her into being; her mother’s spirit passed into her body, and she ought to be Diana to me. Each attempt to throw it off makes this love cling more tightly—this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which blights your hopes and ruins me forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

Neither time nor distance can wrench from my soul what has become a part of it. Since coming here I have not ceased for one instant to feel the hell of passion planted within me, burning until everything is cold, motionless, and dead.
